summary: For ages 12–13, this topic teaches two linked strands: (1) deformation — elastic change returns to shape, inelastic/plastic change is permanent, with the elastic limit as the boundary; and (2) fluid pressure and thermal expansion as consequences of particle behaviour. The central aim is correct MECHANISM over memorised facts: materials expand when heated because particle spacing increases (not because particles swell), and fluid pressure increases with depth and acts in all directions (normal to every surface). The guidance aims to address two documented misconceptions — 'particles get bigger' and the 1D 'a heated ring's hole must shrink' intuition — using a 2D particle/spring picture intended to help learners reason about all particles spreading together (its effectiveness is proposed, not established by the cited sources). Activities move from hands-on contrasting cases through particle-level pictures to applications (bridge/rail gaps, divers, dams) and consolidating checks.
misconceptions: Thinking the particles themselves get bigger when a material is heated, rather than the SPACING between them increasing while particle size stays constant.
Reasoning in 1D that a heated ring's hole must shrink as the metal grows inward — it actually expands, because every particle moves outward uniformly from its neighbours.
Treating 'bridges have expansion gaps' as a fact to recall rather than a consequence of particles spreading when heated.
Confusing elastic and plastic deformation, or assuming all stretching is reversible — not recognising the elastic limit beyond which shape change is permanent.
Believing pressure in a liquid acts only downward, rather than in all directions and normal to every surface, increasing with depth.
Thinking atmospheric pressure is constant or increases with height, rather than decreasing as the weight of air above decreases.
Assuming heavier or larger objects always sink and lighter ones float, ignoring upthrust and the role of density.

activities.title: Stretch it, bend it: feeling elastic vs plastic
steps: Handle a contrasting pair of objects: stretch a rubber band and release it (returns to shape), then bend a paperclip or squash some plasticine (stays changed).

State for each object whether the change was reversible, then sort a set of objects (rubber band, spring, paperclip, clay, sponge) into 'returns to shape' (elastic) and 'stays changed' (inelastic/plastic).

Load a spring with increasing force, removing the load after each addition to check whether it returns to its original length; the elastic limit lies between the last load it fully recovered from and the first load that left it permanently stretched.
Write a one-sentence definition distinguishing elastic from plastic deformation, using the term 'elastic limit'.
activities.insight: Elastic deformation returns to the original shape when the force is removed; inelastic/plastic deformation is permanent. The elastic limit is the boundary beyond which shape change becomes permanent — so not all stretching is reversible.

activities.title: Why heated things grow: spacing, not swelling
steps: Look at or build a two-panel particle picture of a solid: a 'cold' lattice and a 'hot' lattice, where the particle DOTS are drawn the same size in both.
Describe out loud what changes from cold to hot (particles vibrate more and move further apart) and what stays the same (the size of each particle).
Explain in writing why a metal bar gets longer when heated, using the word 'spacing'.
Predict what happens to the bar as it cools, then check against the model.
activities.insight: Materials expand when heated because the particles vibrate more and the SPACING between them increases, while the particles themselves stay the same size. Expansion is increased separation, not swollen particles.

activities.title: The ring-and-hole puzzle: does the hole shrink?
steps: Before any demonstration, predict what happens to the hole in a metal plate (or ring) when the whole plate is heated: does the hole get bigger, smaller, or stay the same? Write down the prediction and the reason.
Reason with a 2D picture: draw or view the plate as a grid of particles, and add arrows showing each particle moving outward from its neighbours as it is heated.
Use the radial-spacing arrows to decide what happens to the gap in the middle, then revise the prediction if needed.

Observe the actual result (hole expands) via a ring-and-ball demo — a ball that will not pass through the cool ring passes once the ring is heated, showing the hole has grown — or a heated plate-with-hole if available, and reconcile it with the 2D reasoning.
activities.insight: A heated plate's hole EXPANDS, not shrinks. Because every particle moves outward uniformly from its neighbours, every gap — including the central hole — grows. The 1D 'metal grows inward so the hole closes' intuition fails when you reason in 2D about all particles spreading together.

activities.title: From the fact to the reason: expansion gaps
steps: Look at an image of a railway track or bridge section with a visible gap, and answer 'Why is the gap there?' — not just 'for expansion' but routed through the particle mechanism.
Write an explanation connecting: hot day → particles vibrate more → spacing increases → the metal lengthens → without a gap it would buckle.

Give one more everyday example of thermal expansion either causing a problem or being used usefully (e.g. a metal lid loosened under hot water, or a bimetallic thermostat strip bending — which works because two bonded metals expand by different amounts, i.e. differential expansion, distinct from the single-plate hole demonstration).
activities.insight: Expansion gaps are a consequence of the spacing mechanism, not an isolated fact. Engineers leave gaps because heated metal lengthens as particle spacing grows; without the gap the lengthening would cause buckling.

activities.title: The three-jet bottle: depth and all directions
steps: Look at (or set up) a tall water bottle with three small holes at different heights, taped shut, with the cap removed so air can enter at the top. Before the holes are opened, PREDICT how the three jets will compare and WHY.

Open the holes and observe: compare how fast and how far out each jet pushes from the bottle, measured at the same level just below the lowest hole (or with the bottle raised well above where the water lands), and note which direction the water leaves the holes.
Explain the result using two ideas together: pressure increases with depth (more weight of water above) and pressure acts in all directions (so water squirts sideways).
Draw a depth–pressure diagram: arrows normal to every surface, drawn longer at greater depth; add a separate note that atmospheric pressure DECREASES with height as the weight of air above decreases.
Apply the mechanism to explain why a dam is thicker at the bottom and why a deep-sea diver feels squeezed harder going down.
activities.insight: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because of the weight of fluid above, and at any point it acts in all directions (normal to every surface) — so the bottom jet leaves the bottle fastest, and all jets shoot out sideways, at right angles to the wall. Atmospheric pressure, by contrast, decreases with height because there is less air above.

activities.title: Consolidation check: sort, order, and spot the error
steps: Categorise a set of objects into elastic vs inelastic/plastic deformation.
Order three tank depths by the pressure at each.
Answer: when a metal ring is heated, does the central hole get bigger, smaller, or stay the same? Choose and justify.
Complete the sentence: 'When a solid is heated, the particles vibrate more and move further ____, while the particles themselves stay the same ____.'
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can apply the deformation distinction, depth–pressure ordering, the ring-and-hole result, and the spacing mechanism without prompting.

checkQuestion: A sealed plastic bottle full of water has three identical small holes: one near the top, one in the middle, and one near the bottom. When the water squirts out, how do the three jets compare — and why?
checkAnswer: The bottom jet squirts out hardest and furthest, the middle less, the top least — because pressure in a liquid INCREASES with depth (more weight of water above pushing). And the water squirts OUT sideways through the holes, showing pressure acts in ALL directions at each depth, not just downwards.
